```{python}
# | tags: [setup]
"""Slide figures built from the newest dated snapshot.

The deck reads the same curated snapshot the website is generated from, so a
number on a slide can always be traced back to a row in the public CSVs.
"""

from collections import Counter

import plotly.graph_objects as go
from IPython.display import HTML
from plotly.offline import get_plotlyjs
from plotly.io import to_html

from oss_das.cli import resolve_snapshot_date
from oss_das.core import PATHS, read_csv
from oss_das.site import load_plot_data, metric_lookup

SNAPSHOT_DATE = resolve_snapshot_date(None, prefer_latest=True)
DATA = load_plot_data(SNAPSHOT_DATE)

# Discovery is a much wider net than the curated catalog, and most of it has not
# been looked at yet. Saying so on stage is cheaper than being corrected from the
# floor by someone whose package is in the unreviewed pile.
CANDIDATES = read_csv(PATHS.snapshot(SNAPSHOT_DATE) / "candidates.csv")
# Bare-acronym probes are what reach a package like dastools on an institutional
# GitLab, but "das" also matches German prose and dashboards. Quoting the total
# would dress thousands of unrelated repositories up as an ecosystem, so the
# headline counts only candidates a domain-specific probe actually named.
SPECIFIC = [item for item in CANDIDATES if item["probe_class"] == "domain-specific"]
DISCOVERED = len(SPECIFIC)
SWEPT = len(CANDIDATES)
UNREVIEWED = sum(item["catalog_status"] == "unreviewed" for item in SPECIFIC)

PROJECTS = [item for item in DATA["projects"] if item["status"] == "included"]
WATCHLIST = [item for item in DATA["projects"] if item["status"] == "watchlist"]
REVIEWED = len(DATA["projects"])
INCLUDED = len(PROJECTS)
INCLUDED_IDS = {item["id"] for item in PROJECTS}
VALUES = metric_lookup(DATA["metrics"])

INK = "#13293d"
TEAL = "#087e8b"
CORAL = "#ff5a5f"
COLORWAY = [TEAL, CORAL, "#f5b700", "#5c4d7d", "#4c956c"]

_figure_count = 0


def show(figure: go.Figure, height: int = 470) -> HTML:
    """Render a figure sized for a slide.

    The plotly library itself is emitted separately below. Bundling it with the
    first figure makes Quarto hoist that whole block, div included, out of
    reveal's slide container and onto every slide.
    """
    global _figure_count
    _figure_count += 1
    figure.update_layout(
        template="plotly_white",
        colorway=COLORWAY,
        font={"family": "system-ui, sans-serif", "color": INK, "size": 15},
        margin={"l": 10, "r": 20, "t": 10, "b": 40},
        height=height,
    )
    return HTML(
        to_html(
            figure,
            full_html=False,
            include_plotlyjs=False,
            config={"displaylogo": False, "displayModeBar": False, "responsive": True},
            # A stable id keeps an unchanged rebuild byte-identical.
            div_id=f"slide-figure-{_figure_count}",
        )
    )


def count_flag(field: str) -> int:
    return sum(item[field] == "True" for item in PROJECTS)


def share(count: int) -> str:
    return f"{count} of {INCLUDED}"


def portraits() -> HTML:
    """Render whichever portrait files are actually present in docs/assets.

    Drop a new file in, re-render, and it appears; nothing here needs editing.
    A missing file is skipped rather than left as a broken image on stage.
    """
    wanted = [
        ("github-avatar.png", "github.com/d-chambers"),
        ("linkedin-photo.jpg", "linkedin.com/in/derrick-chambers"),
    ]
    tiles = [
        f'<figure class="portrait"><img src="assets/{name}" alt="{caption}">'
        f"<figcaption>{caption}</figcaption></figure>"
        for name, caption in wanted
        if (PATHS.docs / "assets" / name).exists()
    ]
    return HTML(f'<div class="portrait-row">{"".join(tiles)}</div>')


ON_PYPI = sum(bool(item["pypi_packages"]) for item in PROJECTS)
NO_RELEASE = sum(not item["latest_release_at"] for item in PROJECTS)
# A project whose repository lookup failed carries no push date. Counting the
# projects known to be recent, rather than subtracting the stale ones, keeps an
# unknown from being reported as activity — the same way the flag counts do.
RECENT = sum(
    bool(item["days_since_push"]) and int(item["days_since_push"]) <= 365
    for item in PROJECTS
)
# Licensing is measured, not required for inclusion, so these counts describe
# the ecosystem instead of describing the rule that selected it.
COPYLEFT = sum(
    (item["license_spdx"] or "").startswith(("GPL", "LGPL", "AGPL")) for item in PROJECTS
)
OPEN_SOURCE = sum(item["license_class"] == "osi-approved" for item in PROJECTS)
# The slide title counts the next one, so it cannot go stale as the catalog grows.
NEXT_LIBRARY = INCLUDED + 1
# Stated rather than left for the audience to tally: applying the inclusion
# policy as written makes the speaker's own organisation the largest single
# publisher in the catalog, and a disclosure is worth more with a number on it.
OWNERS = Counter(item["owner"] for item in PROJECTS)
DASDAE_COUNT = OWNERS["DASDAE"]
SOLO_OWNERS = sum(1 for count in OWNERS.values() if count == 1)
NO_LICENSE = sum(item["license_class"] == "unlicensed" for item in PROJECTS)
```

## Why care about tools?

::: {.quotation}
> New directions in science are launched by new tools much more often than by new
> concepts. The effect of a concept-driven revolution is to explain old things in
> new ways. The effect of a tool-driven revolution is to discover new things that
> have to be explained.

::: {.attribution}
Freeman Dyson, *Imagined Worlds* (1997)
:::
:::

. . .

We name whole eras after the tools that set their ceiling — stone, bronze, iron.
This conference is named after a man who did not invent the telescope, but pointed
a better one at the sky.

. . .

Seismology's own version: C and Fortran driven from the shell, then Python, R,
MATLAB and Julia, then shared formats, then shared libraries. ObsPy never
discovered anything by itself. It lowered the barrier, and a generation of
discoveries followed.

## DAS is earlier on that curve

DAS gives us more channels than seismology has ever had, and far less shared
infrastructure to handle them. Several foundational packages have appeared, each
with real strengths — and no guarantee that any two of them fit together.

. . .

::: {.headline}
So: what already exists, and where does it fail to fit?
:::

## How the list was built {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- Candidate discovery from GitHub topics and the DAS literature
- Every candidate is **reviewed by hand** before inclusion — discovery never
  silently promotes a repository
- Included means *reusable software*: a package, framework, or CLI. Not a paper's
  supplementary notebook
- Every value records its source and retrieval time
- A missing metric stays missing. **Never converted to zero**
:::

. . .

::: {.headline}
`{python} DISCOVERED` discovered &rarr; `{python} REVIEWED` reviewed &rarr;
`{python} INCLUDED` included
:::

::: {.provenance}
`{python} len(WATCHLIST)` sit on a watchlist for scope or reusability questions, not
for licensing — and **`{python} UNREVIEWED` candidates are still unreviewed**. A further
`{python} SWEPT - DISCOVERED` repositories matched only a bare-acronym sweep and are
almost all something else called DAS.
This is a floor on the ecosystem, not a census. If your package is missing, that is
a backlog, not a judgement.
:::

## The ecosystem is broader than it feels

```{python}
categories = Counter(item["primary_category"] for item in PROJECTS)
languages = ["Python", "Jupyter Notebook", "Rust", "Julia", ""]
labels = {"": "unspecified", "Jupyter Notebook": "notebooks"}
# Coral is reserved for "thinly covered" elsewhere in the deck, so language
# colours deliberately avoid it.
language_colors = ["#087e8b", "#f5b700", "#5c4d7d", "#4c956c", "#9aa5ab"]
order = [name for name, _ in categories.most_common()][::-1]

figure = go.Figure()
for language, color in zip(languages, language_colors, strict=True):
    counts = [
        sum(
            1
            for item in PROJECTS
            if item["primary_category"] == category and item["language"] == language
        )
        for category in order
    ]
    if not any(counts):
        continue
    figure.add_bar(
        y=[name.replace("-", " ") for name in order],
        x=counts,
        name=labels.get(language, language),
        orientation="h",
        marker_color=color,
        hovertemplate="%{y}<br>%{x} project(s)<extra>%{fullData.name}</extra>",
    )

for category in order:
    figure.add_annotation(
        x=categories[category] + 0.06,
        y=category.replace("-", " "),
        text=str(categories[category]),
        showarrow=False,
        xanchor="left",
        font={"color": INK},
    )

figure.update_layout(
    barmode="stack",
    showlegend=True,
    legend={"orientation": "h", "y": -0.08, "x": 0, "traceorder": "normal"},
    xaxis={
        "title": "",
        "showticklabels": False,
        "showgrid": False,
        "range": [0, max(categories.values()) + 0.45],
    },
    yaxis={"title": ""},
)
show(figure)
```

::: {.provenance}
Primary category is a manual judgement; several projects span more than one.
:::

## And adoption thins out fast

```{python}
# The 30-day window is dominated by a two-day spike immediately before the
# snapshot, which flatters the leader by roughly a factor of four. Six months is
# the honest window here.
downloads = sorted(
    (
        (item["name"], VALUES[(item["id"], "pypi_downloads_180d")])
        for item in PROJECTS
        if (item["id"], "pypi_downloads_180d") in VALUES
    ),
    key=lambda row: row[1],
)

figure = go.Figure(
    go.Bar(
        y=[name for name, _ in downloads],
        x=[value for _, value in downloads],
        orientation="h",
        marker_color=[
            TEAL if value == downloads[-1][1] else "#9fbfc4" for _, value in downloads
        ],
        hovertemplate="%{y}<br>%{x:,.0f} downloads<extra></extra>",
    )
)
figure.update_layout(
    showlegend=False,
    xaxis={"title": "PyPI downloads, previous 180 days"},
    yaxis={"title": ""},
)
show(figure)
```

::: {.provenance}
Registry counts include CI and mirror traffic, so read them as an upper bound on
human use. Only `{python} share(ON_PYPI)` included projects publish to PyPI at all,
and one of those reports no traffic — a blank, not a zero. Conda ships
`{python} sum(bool(i["conda_packages"]) for i in PROJECTS)`. Everything else is clone-and-hope.
:::

## Most of it is research code, not infrastructure

```{python}
checks = [
    ("Documentation", count_flag("has_docs")),
    ("Tests", count_flag("has_tests")),
    ("Continuous integration", count_flag("has_ci")),
    ("Any tagged release", INCLUDED - NO_RELEASE),
    ("Touched in the last year", RECENT),
]

figure = go.Figure()
figure.add_bar(
    y=[label for label, _ in checks][::-1],
    x=[INCLUDED - value for _, value in checks][::-1],
    orientation="h",
    name="absent",
    marker_color="#e8ecee",
    hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x} without<extra></extra>",
)
figure.add_bar(
    y=[label for label, _ in checks][::-1],
    x=[value for _, value in checks][::-1],
    orientation="h",
    name="present",
    marker_color=TEAL,
    text=[f"{value} of {INCLUDED}" for _, value in checks][::-1],
    textposition="inside",
    insidetextanchor="end",
    textfont={"color": "white"},
    hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x} with<extra></extra>",
)
figure.update_layout(
    barmode="stack",
    showlegend=False,
    xaxis={"title": "", "showticklabels": False, "showgrid": False},
    yaxis={"title": ""},
)
show(figure)
```

::: {.provenance}
Signals are detected from repository structure, so they under-count projects that
document or test somewhere unusual. Licensing is recorded rather than required, so
the numbers are a measurement: `{python} share(OPEN_SOURCE)` carry an OSI-approved
license, `{python} share(COPYLEFT)` are copyleft, and `{python} NO_LICENSE` publish
source with no license at all — which grants nobody the right to reuse them.
:::

## What everyone builds, and what nobody does

```{python}
present = Counter(
    row["capability"]
    for row in DATA["capabilities"]
    if row["present"] == "True" and row["project_id"] in INCLUDED_IDS
)
ranked = present.most_common()
singletons = sum(1 for _, value in ranked if value == 1)
top = ranked[:11][::-1]

figure = go.Figure(
    go.Bar(
        y=[name.replace("-", " ") for name, _ in top],
        x=[value for _, value in top],
        orientation="h",
        marker_color=[TEAL if value > 2 else CORAL for _, value in top],
        text=[str(value) for _, value in top],
        textposition="outside",
        cliponaxis=False,
        hovertemplate="%{y}<br>%{x} project(s)<extra></extra>",
    )
)
figure.update_layout(
    showlegend=False,
    xaxis={
        "title": "",
        "showticklabels": False,
        "showgrid": False,
        "range": [0, max(present.values()) + 0.7],
    },
    yaxis={"title": ""},
)
show(figure, height=420)
```

::: {.headline}
`{python} singletons` of `{python} len(ranked)` capabilities have exactly one implementation.
:::

::: {.provenance}
Curated tags, not feature audits. If that one project stops, the capability leaves
the ecosystem with it.
:::

## The gaps that actually hurt {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- **Interoperability** — every library invented its own data model. The fix is
  conversion between them, not consolidation into one
- **Metadata** — there is a standard proposal, and almost no tooling that enforces it
- **GPU acceleration** — DAS volumes outgrew single-threaded NumPy years ago
- **Large-scale visualization** — nobody can look at a full survey interactively
:::

## Build library `{python} NEXT_LIBRARY`, if you want to {.smaller}

A second implementation is not the problem. Competition is how a better data model,
a faster reader, or a nicer API actually arrives — and the earlier chart shows a
field that is *under*-built, not over-built.

. . .

What costs us is work nobody else can pick up: no license, no docs, no release, a
data model nothing can read. That is not fragmentation, it is evaporation.

. . .

**If you use these tools:** cite the software, report the bugs, send the patch.

**If you write them:** publish to a registry, choose a license deliberately, and
treat your data structures as a public interface — a converter can only reach what
it can see.

. . .

::: {.headline}
The bar is not "don't build it." The bar is "build it so someone else can use it."
:::

## Coding agents change the arithmetic {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- The cost of *writing* a DAS library just fell through the floor
- More tools is fine. More **unmaintained** tools is the risk
- Agents write against whatever they can read — clear APIs, real docstrings,
  honest error messages
- The libraries that are legible to an agent are about to get used far more than
  the ones that are not
:::

. . .

::: {.headline}
Documentation is no longer only for humans.
:::

## Four experiments {.smaller}

Each of these started as a gap on the earlier slide. All are recent, and all were
built far faster than I could have built them three years ago.

::: {.incremental}
- **unidas** — convert between the data structures of the major libraries, so the
  choice of library stops being a lock-in
- **Inventory** — shared metadata handling that matches the emerging standard
- **DASJax** — GPU and autodiff-capable processing
- **DerZug** — large-scale visualization for data you cannot fit on a screen
:::

. . .

None of these needs to be built by me. I would rather be out-competed than be the
only option.

## Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
1. There are more DAS tools than you think — and fewer than you need
2. The ecosystem is one library deep in most niches, and zero deep in some
3. The gap is not algorithms. It is the boring infrastructure between them
4. Agents make building cheap, which makes *finishing* the hard part
:::

. . .

::: {.headline}
Build the thing. Publish the tool, not just the paper.
:::
